name: Nicotinamide riboside
lead: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a pyridine-nucleoside and a form of vitamin B3 that serves as a precursor to the coenzyme NAD+ [1]. Inside cells it is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which is then converted to NAD+ by NMNAT enzymes, bypassing other known NAD+ synthesis routes [1]. It is sold as an oral supplement under brands such as Tru Niagen and is closely related to, and often compared with, NMN [1][2].

NR is marketed for healthy ageing, energy and cellular health, on the premise that NAD+ declines with age and that supplementing precursors restores it [3][4]. Randomised trials consistently show that oral NR raises blood NAD+ metabolites, but a 2023 review concluded that evidence that raising NAD+ improves physiological function in people is unclear [5]. Trials in conditions such as mild cognitive impairment, Parkinson's disease, COPD, kidney disease and peripheral artery disease have mostly established safety and tolerability, with variable functional effects [6][7][8][9][10].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities NR appears in supplement lists, with some users reporting increased energy and others using it as part of longevity stacks alongside resveratrol and quercetin [11][12].

paras: The molecular weight of NR is 255.25 g/mol, and 290.70 g/mol for its chloride salt, so 100 mg of NR chloride supplies about 88 mg of NR [1]. NR chloride degrades above about 130 degrees Celsius into nicotinamide and ribose and breaks down faster at neutral than at acidic pH, which affects how it is formulated and stored [1].

NR was described in bacteria in 1944 as a growth factor for Haemophilus influenzae, which depends on salvage of NAD precursors from its environment [1]. Pellagra, the first disease linked to NAD deficiency, was tied to nutrition by Joseph Goldberger in 1914 and to niacin deficiency by Conrad Elvehjem in 1937, leading to identification of nicotinic acid and nicotinamide as precursors [1]. In 2004 NR was reported as an additional NAD precursor in eukaryotes, and it is now recognised as a vitamin B3 form present in cow and human milk [1].

ChromaDex licensed patents for NR from Dartmouth College, Cornell University and Washington University in St Louis in 2012 and developed a production process for NR chloride, branded Niagen. The company was in a patent dispute with Elysium Health over NR supplements between 2016 and 2023 and was renamed Niagen Bioscience in 2025 [1]. A 2016 Nature Communications paper reported that NR is orally bioavailable in mice and humans [13].

NR is promoted for energy and healthy ageing rather than direct changes to appearance, and no published trial reviewed here measures facial or skin appearance outcomes. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis examined NMN and NR for skeletal muscle mass and function [14]. Forum users report taking NR for energy, with one describing the results as pricey but strong [12].

NR is not approved as a drug. It has been tested in clinical studies of neurological disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, peripheral artery disease, COPD, mitochondrial disease, ataxia-telangiectasia and lupus [6][7][8][9][10][15][16][17][18].

NAD+ is a coenzyme for redox reactions and a substrate for sirtuins, PARPs and CD38; its levels fall with age in several tissues in animal models, and restoring NAD+ in old or diseased animals has improved function and, in some models, lifespan [3][4]. NR and NMN are the two best-studied precursors, and reviews note they may behave differently depending on tissue expression of NAD-synthesising enzymes [2]. Reviews also caution that much of NAD+ biology is poorly understood and that animal results may not translate to humans [19][5].
A 2025 study reported that NR and NMN facilitate NAD+ synthesis through enterohepatic circulation, indicating that gut and liver processing shape how precursors reach tissues [20].

A 2023 review of human supplementation with NAD+-boosting compounds concluded that oral NR and NMN raise NAD+ levels but that the evidence that this improves physiological function is unclear [5]. A long-term randomised, placebo-controlled trial of NR chloride in healthy overweight adults assessed safety and metabolism [21].

In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, a 10-week randomised pilot of 20 participants with dose escalation to 1 g per day had safety as its primary objective [6]. The NADPARK phase I trial gave 1,000 mg NR or placebo for 30 days to 30 newly diagnosed Parkinson's patients; NR was well tolerated and increased cerebral NAD levels, with variable response [7]. Randomised trials have also examined airway inflammation in COPD, a crossover of CoQ10 and NR in chronic kidney disease, and walking performance in peripheral artery disease [8][9][10]. A registered trial is testing NR for arterial stiffness and elevated blood pressure in advanced CKD [22]. Several registered studies in heart failure were small or terminated early [23][24][15].
No randomised trial among those reviewed tested NR for facial appearance or aesthetic outcomes.

Trials in healthy and diseased populations have generally reported that NR was well tolerated at the doses studied, with occasional mild nausea, flushing or digestive complaints reported with niacin-family compounds [6][7][21]. Long-term safety data beyond months are limited [5]. The US FDA accepted a GRAS notice for NR chloride in 2016 and recognised it as a new dietary ingredient in 2015 and 2017, and the EU authorised it as a novel food in food supplements in 2020; Wikipedia notes these decisions relied on safety dossiers supplied by the manufacturer [1].

The NR market has been shaped by patent litigation between ChromaDex and Elysium Health between 2016 and 2023 [1]. In forums, NR and NMN are often discussed interchangeably, with some users switching from NR to NMN because of cost [12]. One TRT forum user lists NR hydrogen malate alongside resveratrol, quercetin and beetroot in a daily regimen [11].

lore.intro: NR is discussed in forums as a premium NAD+ booster for energy and longevity, frequently compared with NMN on price and effect [12].

claims.believers: A user described incredible energy from NR and moved to cheaper NMN hoping for the same [12].
claims.experts: Trials show NR raises NAD+ metabolites, but a review found it unclear whether this improves physiological function [5].

claims.claim: NR slows ageing by restoring NAD+
claims.believers: Proponents point to age-related NAD+ decline and animal results [3][4].
claims.experts: Rodent data are positive in several models, while human data are limited and reviews describe translation as unproven [4][5].

claims.claim: NR is safe for long-term stacking with resveratrol and other supplements
claims.believers: Forum users include it in daily regimens with resveratrol, quercetin and others [11].
claims.experts: Trials report good tolerability in the weeks to months studied, but long-term safety and interaction data are limited [21][5].
